turns.content: Tariq has been my best friend since seventh grade, but since he lost his design job nine months ago he's basically vanished into his parents' basement. He ignores Discord, won't pick up calls, and last week when I dropped off some art supplies he snapped at me and said I was "trying to fix him." I'm exhausted. I've been reading these forums about stonewalling and weaponized apathy, and I'm starting to suspect he's doing this deliberately — like the silence itself is a message. Board game night is Saturday. I want to draft a casual text inviting him, something low-pressure, but honestly I don't know if I'm being naive or if this is the last time I should try.

You’ve kept reaching out to a friend you’ve had since seventh grade, and getting silence—and then being snapped at—sounds exhausting. It’s reasonable to want to leave the door open without making yourself responsible for getting him through it.

**His withdrawal is clear; his motive isn’t.** Losing his job and pulling away could reflect shame, depression, overwhelm, or wanting space. There isn’t enough here to conclude that he’s deliberately using silence to hurt you. His comment about “fixing him” does suggest that practical help isn’t landing as you intended, even though you meant it kindly.

For Saturday, keep it about spending time together, not helping him recover:

> Hey Tariq, we’re doing board games Saturday at [time] at [place]. You’re welcome to join—would be good to hang out. No pressure, and no need to reply if you’re sitting this one out.

Sending that isn’t naive. It’s one invitation, not a commitment to keep chasing. Afterward, let it stand: no reminder, follow-up call, or surprise visit. If he doesn’t respond, you can step back without deciding that the friendship is permanently over—or that he’s a bad friend by intent. **You don’t have to prove he means harm to recognize that this pattern is wearing you down.**

Nine months of marked withdrawal is concerning, though it doesn’t establish a diagnosis or an emergency. If you have separate reasons to think he’s unsafe—such as talk of suicide or not being able to meet basic needs—contact someone close to him who can check on him rather than relying on a game-night invitation.

My recommendation: send one ordinary, low-pressure invitation, then give him space and yourself permission to stop initiating for now.

I appreciate that you're not feeding me the "he's punishing you" narrative, even though part of me wanted you to. It's easier to be angry than to sit with what you actually said — that I don't know his motives, only his absence.

The text draft is good. Two things. First, I don't know if I should name the game or leave it vague so he can say yes without knowing what he's agreeing to. Second — and this is the part I hate admitting — if he ignores this one, do I just stop? Ten years of friendship feels like it deserves more ceremony than a silent phone.

You’re making a hard distinction: his absence hurts, even though you don’t know what it means. And after ten years, wanting something more deliberate than simply letting the messages die makes sense.

**Name the game if you’ve chosen it.** Knowing what he’s being invited to makes the decision easier; vagueness doesn’t make an invitation lower-pressure. If plans are flexible, say that honestly.

> Hey Tariq, board games at [place] Saturday at [time]—we’re planning on [game]. Would be good to hang out if you feel like coming. No pressure, and no need to reply if you’re skipping this one.

**If he ignores it, stop pursuing a response—but you don’t have to declare the friendship over.** Those are different decisions. You can stop calling, dropping things off, and organizing your attention around whether he answers, while remaining open to hearing from him.

I’d keep that boundary out of the invitation. “This is my last attempt” would turn Saturday into a test he doesn’t know how to pass.

If the invitation goes unanswered and you still need to mark the change, a separate message later is reasonable—not as another attempt to get a response, but to say plainly what you’re doing:

> You’ve been my best friend for ten years, and I miss you. I’m going to step back from checking in rather than keep reaching out. I care about you, and I’m open to hearing from you. You don’t need to reply to this.

You don’t owe that extra message, and it may not produce the acknowledgment you want. But it can give your decision words without assigning him motives or demanding a goodbye. The friendship deserves care; that doesn’t require unlimited attempts from you.

My recommendation is to send the specific invitation, let Saturday pass without chasing, and then take a break from initiating. Use the separate message only if saying it matters to you even knowing he might remain silent.

You're right that I shouldn't turn Saturday into a test he doesn't know he's taking. That distinction — stopping the pursuit versus declaring the friendship over — is hard to hold onto when I'm this tired, but it's honest.

If he ignores this, I think I need that separate message you described. Not to get a response, just to say something true out loud. Can we draft it now so I have it ready?

Yes. You want to mark the change rather than leave ten years of friendship to an unanswered phone—not make one more bid for a reply.

> Hey Tariq. You’ve been my best friend for ten years, and that means a lot to me. I miss you. Not hearing back has been hard, so I’m going to step back from reaching out for now. I care about you, and I’d be glad to hear from you if you want to reconnect. You don’t need to reply to this—I just wanted to let you know where I’m at.

My recommendation: keep this separate from Saturday’s invitation and don’t send it immediately after game night. Let a few days pass, reread it, and send it if it still expresses what you mean—even if no answer comes. Then follow through on giving yourself that break.

Thanks. That draft is almost exactly what I'd want to say. One thing though — "not hearing back has been hard" feels like it undersells it. It's not just hard. It's nine months of watching someone I love disappear and wondering if I did something wrong. Can we adjust that line so it's honest without being accusatory?

Yes—“hard” leaves out both how long this has lasted and the self-doubt it’s brought up. You can name that impact without claiming he intended it.

> Hey Tariq. You’ve been my best friend for ten years, and that means a lot to me. I miss you. These past nine months, I’ve felt sad and disconnected from you, and I’ve found myself wondering whether I did something wrong. I don’t know what things have been like for you, but continuing to reach out without hearing back has been wearing me down. I’m going to step back from reaching out for now. I care about you, and I’d be glad to hear from you if you want to reconnect. You don’t need to reply to this—I just wanted to let you know where I’m at.

My recommendation is to keep “wondering whether I did something wrong” as a statement of your experience, rather than turning it into a question he needs to answer. It tells the fuller truth without making your boundary depend on an explanation.

That line is better. "I've felt sad and disconnected" and "wondering whether I did something wrong" — that says what actually happened without making it a charge. I'll send the invitation Saturday morning and keep the separate message ready.

You’ve found wording that names both the loss and the self-doubt without claiming to know his motives. That matters when you’re this tired.

One practical adjustment: if the game and time are already set, I’d send the invitation before Saturday morning so he has more notice. Then let it stand without following up. Keep the separate message for a few days after game night, and reread it before sending—you can take space whether or not you decide you need to say it out loud.
